n: John introduces Lazarus of Bethany, the brother of Mary and Martha — close friends of Jesus. Bethany was a village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives.

f.g: A form of the Hebrew Eleazar, “God has helped.”

n: John identifies this Mary as the one who anointed Jesus’s feet and wiped them with her hair — an event he will narrate in the next chapter, assuming his readers already know the story.
The sisters send a simple message: “Lord, the one you love is sick.” They don’t demand anything; they trust his love to act.

f.g: Some have suggested Lazarus may be the unnamed “beloved disciple,” but most identify that disciple as John.

n: Jesus says the sickness won’t end in death but will bring glory to God and to the Son. Lazarus will die, but death won’t have the last word.
John emphasizes that Jesus truly loved Martha, Mary, and Lazarus — so his delay that follows is not indifference.

f.g: John uses agapaō here, the word for deep, committed love.

n: Yet Jesus waits two more days where he is. Sometimes divine delays serve a greater purpose than an immediate answer would.
Then he tells the disciples they will go back to Judea.

f.g: The southern region containing Jerusalem and Bethany.

n: The disciples are alarmed: the leaders there just tried to stone him. Why go back?
Jesus answers with a proverb: there are twelve hours of daylight; someone walking by day doesn’t stumble because they can see. His day of work isn’t over yet.

f.g: Daylight was divided into twelve hours, varying in length with the seasons.

n: Stumbling happens in the dark, when one has no light. Walking with Christ is walking in the light.

f.w: there is no light in him

n: Jesus says their friend Lazarus has “fallen asleep,” and he is going to wake him.

f.g: Early Christians often called death “sleep,” since believers will awake in the Resurrection.

n: The disciples take him literally: if Lazarus is sleeping, he’ll recover.

f.g: Literally “he will be saved” — he will get better.

n: John explains the misunderstanding: Jesus meant death, but they thought he meant ordinary rest.

f.g: Howbeit = however.

n: So Jesus tells them plainly: Lazarus is dead.

f.g: Jesus knew this without being told.

n: He is glad, for their sake, that he wasn’t there to prevent it, because what they are about to see will strengthen their faith.

f.w: to the intent ye may believe

n: Thomas, called “the Twin,” bravely urges the others to go along and die with Jesus. Remembered as a doubter, he here shows courageous loyalty.

f.g: Greek for “twin,” the same meaning as the Aramaic name Thomas.

f.w: that we may die with him

n: When Jesus arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Some Jews believed the soul lingered near the body for three days, so by day four death seemed final.

f.g: The detail stresses that Lazarus was truly and irreversibly dead by human standards.

n: Bethany was close to Jerusalem — about two miles away.

f.g: About 1¾ to 2 miles (roughly 3 km).

n: Many people from Jerusalem had come to comfort the sisters, as Jewish mourning customs encouraged.

f.g: Mourning traditionally lasted seven days, with friends visiting the grieving family.

n: Martha, ever the active one, hurries out to meet Jesus, while Mary stays seated in the house, perhaps overwhelmed by grief.

f.w: Mary sat still in the house
f.g: Mourners customarily sat on the floor.

n: Martha speaks with honest grief: if Jesus had been there, her brother wouldn’t have died.

f.g: Both sisters say exactly the same words (verse 32) — they had surely said it to each other many times.

n: Yet her faith shines through: even now, she knows God will give Jesus whatever he asks.
Jesus promises her that her brother will rise again.
Martha takes this as the familiar comfort that Lazarus will rise at the final resurrection, a doctrine the Pharisees taught.

f.w: the resurrection at the last day

n: Jesus brings the doctrine into the present: he himself is the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in him will live, even after dying.

f.w: I am the resurrection, and the life

n: And whoever lives believing in him will never truly die. Then he asks her directly, “Do you believe this?”

f.g: Jesus invites a personal testimony, not just agreement with a doctrine.

n: Martha answers with a full confession of faith: Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, the one who was to come into the world — a testimony equal to Peter’s.

f.w: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God

n: Martha quietly goes to fetch Mary, telling her privately that the Teacher has come and is asking for her.

f.w: The Master is come, and calleth for thee

n: Mary gets up at once and goes to him.

f.g: Her quick response shows her devotion despite her grief.

n: Jesus is still outside the village where Martha met him, perhaps to see the sisters away from the crowd.

f.w: not yet come into the town
f.g: Possibly near the tomb, which would have been outside the village.

n: The mourners in the house see Mary rush out and follow, assuming she is going to the tomb to weep.

f.g: Visiting the tomb to mourn was customary during the days after burial.

n: Mary falls at Jesus’s feet — where she is always found in the Gospels — and repeats the same heartbroken words as Martha.

f.w: she fell down at his feet

n: Seeing Mary and the others weeping, Jesus is deeply moved and stirred within. The Greek suggests intense emotion — perhaps even indignation at death and the sorrow it causes.

f.g: Greek embrimaomai — to be deeply moved, to snort with strong emotion.

n: He asks where they have buried Lazarus, and they invite him to “come and see.”
The shortest verse in the Bible: Jesus wept. Even knowing he would raise Lazarus within minutes, he shared their grief. Christ does not stand apart from our sorrow.
Onlookers are touched by how much he loved Lazarus.
Others wonder why the man who healed the blind couldn’t have kept his friend from dying — a question many grieving people still ask.

f.w: which opened the eyes of the blind

n: Deeply moved again, Jesus comes to the tomb — a cave with a large stone across its entrance.

f.w: It was a cave, and a stone lay upon it
f.g: Wealthier families used rock-cut tombs sealed with heavy stones.

n: Jesus orders the stone removed. Practical Martha objects: after four days, the smell will be terrible.

f.g: Bodies were not embalmed; decay would be well underway.

n: Jesus reminds her of his promise: if she believes, she will see God’s glory.

f.w: thou shouldest see the glory of God

n: They roll away the stone. Jesus looks up and thanks his Father for already hearing him — giving thanks before the miracle is visible.

f.w: Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me

n: Jesus knows the Father always hears him; he prays aloud so the onlookers will believe the Father sent him.
Then with a loud voice he commands: “Lazarus, come out!” One day his voice will call all the dead from their graves.

The dead man walks out, still wrapped in burial cloths, his face covered with a cloth. Jesus tells them to unwrap him and set him free. Lazarus was restored to mortal life; he would die again someday, unlike Jesus in his resurrection.

f.g: Strips of linen wound around the body with spices.
napkin = a cloth used to cover the face.

f.w: Loose him, and let him go
f.g: Some see a picture of how Christ frees us from the bonds of sin and death.

n: Many of the mourners who saw this put their faith in Jesus.
But some go and report the miracle to the Pharisees — a sign that evidence alone doesn’t change hearts.

f.w: went their ways to the Pharisees

n: The chief priests and Pharisees call a meeting of the Sanhedrin. They admit Jesus is doing many miracles — yet ask only what they should do about it.

f.g: The Sanhedrin, the 71-member supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem.

n: Their fear is political: if everyone believes in him, the Romans might see a messianic uprising and destroy the temple (“our place”) and the nation.

f.w: take away both our place and nation
f.g: Ironically, the Romans did destroy the temple and Jerusalem in AD 70.

n: Caiaphas, high priest that year, speaks bluntly and rudely to the council: they understand nothing.

f.g: High priest from about AD 18 to 36, son-in-law of Annas.

n: His cold logic: better for one man to die than for the whole nation to be destroyed.

f.g: expedient = advantageous, in one’s interest.

n: John sees divine irony: without realizing it, Caiaphas, by virtue of his office, prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation — words true in a far deeper sense than he intended.
And Jesus would die not only for Israel but to gather God’s scattered children everywhere into one.

f.w: gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad

n: From that day the leaders formally plot to put Jesus to death. Giving life to Lazarus seals Jesus’s own death sentence.

f.w: took counsel together for to put him to death

n: Jesus stops moving openly in Judea and withdraws with his disciples to a town called Ephraim, near the wilderness north of Jerusalem.

f.g: Probably modern et-Taiyibeh, about 12–15 miles northeast of Jerusalem.

n: The Passover is near, and many pilgrims come to Jerusalem early to complete purification rites before the feast.
Standing in the temple, people look for Jesus and speculate whether he will dare come to the festival.

f.w: he will not come to the feast?

n: The chief priests and Pharisees have ordered anyone who knows his whereabouts to report it so they can arrest him. The stage is set for his final Passover.

f.g: shew = show, report.
